prompt: Explain how U.S. health insurance works using only fantasy football metaphors. Keep going long after the metaphor collapses.
response:
Alright, let’s draft this.

Imagine you’re the General Manager of your own life—Team You. Your goal every season (year) is to make the playoffs (survive) and ideally win the championship (thrive). But you can’t do it alone; you need a roster of healthcare providers. To afford them, you need to enter the U.S. Health Insurance Fantasy League.

**The Draft (Open Enrollment)**
Once a year, you have a draft window. This is when you select your insurance plan. You’re not picking individual doctors; you’re picking a *conference* of providers (a network). You have a few different league formats to choose from. There’s the PPO league (Preferred Provider Organization), which is like a dynasty league with a huge waiver wire—you can pick up almost any player (doctor) you want, anytime, even if they’re not in your starting lineup, but the buy-in is massive and the transaction fees are high. Then there’s the HMO league (Health Maintenance Organization), which is a strict salary cap league. You draft a primary care physician (your QB1) and they call all the plays. You want to see a specialist? Your QB1 has to audible to it and throw you a referral pass. If you try to lateral to a dermatologist without that pass, the play is dead, the points don’t count, and you owe the league a penalty fee.

**The Salary Cap and Contract Structure**
Your league buy-in is the annual premium. This is a guaranteed, sunk cost taken out of your paycheck before you even make your first waiver claim. But here’s the kicker: paying the buy-in doesn’t actually put any players on your roster. It just gives you the right to field a team without the league commissioner (the government) fining you into oblivion. Once you’ve paid, you’re given a contract structure that looks like this: a Deductible, Copays, and Co-insurance.

The Deductible is your team’s initial performance threshold. You, the GM, are solely responsible for covering all your players’ points (medical costs) out of your own pocket until your team’s total fantasy score hits, say, 1,500 points.
